blocks.body:
In a vector space you can add vectors and multiply them by scalars from a field. Allowing the scalars to come from a ring gives a module. That small change covers a surprising amount: every abelian group is a module over $\mathbb{Z}$ (with $n\cdot g = g+\dots+g$), and a vector space together with a linear operator $T$ is a module over the polynomial ring $F[x]$, where $x$ acts as $T$.

Modules can be far messier than vector spaces, but over a principal ideal domain the finitely generated ones are completely classified. This page states and proves that structure theorem via the Smith normal form of a matrix, then reads off two classical results: the classification of finitely generated abelian groups, and the canonical forms of a linear operator. It assumes [[ufds|PIDs and unique factorisation]] and [[linear-maps]].

blocks.title: Module
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$. An $R$-module is an abelian group $(M,+)$ with a scalar multiplication $R\times M\to M$ such that, for all $r,s\in R$ and $m,n\in M$,
$$r(m+n) = rm+rn,\quad (r+s)m = rm+sm,\quad (rs)m = r(sm),\quad 1m = m.$$
A submodule is a subgroup closed under scalar multiplication; homomorphisms are additive maps with $\varphi(rm) = r\varphi(m)$; the quotient $M/N$ by a submodule is a module in the same way as a [[dual-spaces|quotient space]].

Examples: $R^n$; any ideal $I\subseteq R$ (the submodules of $R$ are exactly its ideals); $R/I$; abelian groups as $\mathbb{Z}$-modules; and $V_T$, a vector space $V$ over $F$ made into an $F[x]$-module by $p(x)\cdot v = p(T)v$.

blocks.title: What changes when scalars cannot be divided
blocks.body:
$M$ is finitely generated if $M = Rm_1+\dots+Rm_n$ for some elements $m_i$, and free with basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$ if every element is uniquely $\sum r_ie_i$, so that $M\cong R^n$. Over a field every module is free. Over a ring, three new phenomena appear.

1. Torsion. In the $\mathbb{Z}$-module $\mathbb{Z}/6$, the nonzero scalar $6$ kills every element. An element $m$ is torsion if $rm = 0$ for some nonzero $r$; torsion elements can never be part of a basis, so $\mathbb{Z}/6$ is not free.
2. Independent sets need not extend to bases. In $\mathbb{Z}$, the single element $2$ is linearly independent but no basis of $\mathbb{Z}$ contains it.
3. Generating sets need not shrink to bases. $\{2, 3\}$ generates $\mathbb{Z}$, yet neither element alone does, and the pair is not independent ($3\cdot2 - 2\cdot3 = 0$).

Over a PID the damage is limited: one can prove that every submodule of $R^n$ is free of rank at most $n$ (by induction on $n$, projecting onto the last coordinate, whose image is an ideal and hence principal). In particular submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated.

blocks.title: Smith normal form
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a PID and $A$ an $m\times n$ matrix over $R$. There are invertible matrices $P$ ($m\times m$) and $Q$ ($n\times n$) over $R$ with
$$PAQ = \begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_k) & 0\\ 0 & 0\end{pmatrix},\qquad d_1\mid d_2\mid\cdots\mid d_k,\ d_i\neq0.$$
The $d_i$ are unique up to units: $d_1d_2\cdots d_j$ is the gcd of all $j\times j$ minors of $A$, and $k = \operatorname{rank}A$.

blocks.title: Proof for a Euclidean domain
blocks.body:
Use three kinds of invertible row and column operations: swapping two rows (or columns), multiplying one by a unit, and adding a multiple of one row (column) to another. Each is multiplication by an invertible matrix on the left (right).

If $A = 0$ we are done. Otherwise move a nonzero entry of smallest norm to position $(1,1)$. Divide every other entry of the first column by it: $a_{i1} = qa_{11}+r$; subtracting $q$ times row $1$ from row $i$ leaves $r$. If some $r\neq0$, it has smaller norm than $a_{11}$; move it to the corner and start again. Since norms are non-negative integers this cannot go on forever, so eventually the first column, and likewise the first row, are zero apart from $a_{11}$. If some other entry $a_{ij}$ is not divisible by $a_{11}$, add row $i$ to row $1$ and repeat; the remainder of $a_{ij}$ again lowers the corner norm. We end with $a_{11}$ dividing every remaining entry, and induct on the smaller block, whose entries stay multiples of $a_{11}$. (For a general PID, replace each division step by a Bézout step: if $g = \gcd(a,b) = sa+tb$, the invertible matrix $\begin{pmatrix}s&t\\-b/g&a/g\end{pmatrix}$ sends the column $(a,b)$ to $(g,0)$; the number of prime factors of the corner entry then plays the role of the norm.)

Uniqueness: an elementary operation does not change the ideal generated by the $j\times j$ minors (each new minor is a combination of old ones, and the operation can be reversed). For the diagonal matrix that ideal is generated by $d_1\cdots d_j$, using the divisibility chain.

blocks.title: Structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a PID
blocks.body:
Let $R$ be a PID and $M$ a finitely generated $R$-module. Then
$$M\cong R^r\oplus R/(a_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(a_m)$$
for some $r\ge0$ and nonzero non-units $a_1\mid a_2\mid\cdots\mid a_m$. The rank $r$ and the ideals $(a_i)$, the invariant factors, are uniquely determined by $M$. Splitting each $a_i$ into prime powers by the [[crt|Chinese remainder theorem]], $R/(p_1^{e_1}\cdots p_t^{e_t})\cong R/(p_1^{e_1})\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(p_t^{e_t})$, gives the equivalent elementary divisor form, a sum of $R^r$ and cyclic modules $R/(p^e)$.

blocks.title: Proof of existence, and outline of uniqueness
blocks.body:
Choose generators $m_1,\dots,m_n$ and let $\pi: R^n\to M$ send $e_i\mapsto m_i$. Its kernel $K$, the module of relations, is a submodule of $R^n$, hence finitely generated; write its generators as the rows of a matrix $A$. Then $M\cong R^n/K$, where $K$ is the row space of $A$.

Row operations on $A$ change the generators of $K$ but not $K$. Column operations correspond to changing the basis of $R^n$, which replaces $M$ by an isomorphic presentation. So we may replace $A$ by its Smith normal form. With relations $d_1e_1' = 0, \dots, d_ke_k' = 0$ in a new basis $e_1',\dots,e_n'$, the quotient is
$$R^n/K\cong R/(d_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus R/(d_k)\oplus R^{n-k}.$$
Summands with $d_i$ a unit are zero and can be dropped, leaving the stated form with $r = n-k$.

Uniqueness, in outline: $r$ is the dimension of $M\otimes_R F$ over the field of fractions $F$ of $R$ (torsion dies in $F$), and for each prime $p$ the number of $a_i$ divisible by $p^j$ equals the dimension over the field $R/(p)$ of $p^{j-1}T/p^jT$, where $T$ is the torsion submodule. These numbers depend only on $M$.

blocks.title: An abelian group from generators and relations
blocks.body: (a) Identify the abelian group with generators $x, y$ and relations $4x+6y = 0$, $6x+4y = 0$. (b) Do the same for generators $x,y,z$ and relations $2x+4z = 0$, $6y+6z = 0$, $2x+6y+10z = 0$.
blocks.solution:
(a) The relation matrix is $A = \begin{pmatrix}4&6\\6&4\end{pmatrix}$. Subtract column $1$ from column $2$: $\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\6&-2\end{pmatrix}$; swap the columns: $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\-2&6\end{pmatrix}$; add row $1$ to row $2$: $\begin{pmatrix}2&4\\0&10\end{pmatrix}$; subtract twice column $1$ from column $2$: $\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&10\end{pmatrix}$. So the group is
$$\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/10\ \cong\ \mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/5,$$
of order $20 = |\det A|$. The minors confirm it: the gcd of the entries is $d_1 = 2$ and $d_1d_2 = |\det A| = 20$.

(b) Here $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&0&4\\0&6&6\\2&6&10\end{pmatrix}$. The third row is the sum of the first two, so $\det A = 0$ and the rank is $2$. The gcd of the entries is $2$, and the gcd of the $2\times2$ minors is $12$ (for instance the minors $12$ and $-24$ occur, and all are multiples of $12$). Hence $d_1 = 2$, $d_2 = 6$, and the group is $\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z}$: infinite, with free rank $1$ and torsion subgroup of order $12$.

blocks.title: All abelian groups of order 72
blocks.body: List all abelian groups of order $72$ up to isomorphism, in both invariant factor and elementary divisor form.
blocks.solution:
A finite abelian group has $r=0$, and by the elementary divisor form it is a product of its Sylow subgroups, one for each prime. Since $72 = 2^3\cdot3^2$, the $2$-part is $\mathbb{Z}/8$, $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ or $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3$ (one for each partition of $3$) and the $3$-part is $\mathbb{Z}/9$ or $(\mathbb{Z}/3)^2$ (partitions of $2$). That gives $3\times2 = 6$ groups. To get invariant factors, combine the largest prime powers into $a_m$, the next largest into $a_{m-1}$, and so on:
- $\mathbb{Z}/8\oplus\mathbb{Z}/9 \cong \mathbb{Z}/72$
- $\mathbb{Z}/8\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3 \cong \mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/24$
- $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/9\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/36$
- $\mathbb{Z}/4\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3\cong\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z}/12$
- $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3\oplus\mathbb{Z}/9\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/18$
- $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3\oplus(\mathbb{Z}/3)^2\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6\oplus\mathbb{Z}/6$

In general the number of abelian groups of order $\prod p_i^{e_i}$ is $\prod p(e_i)$, where $p(e)$ is the number of [[partitions]] of $e$.

blocks.title: Linear operators as $F[x]$-modules
blocks.body:
Let $T$ act on $V = F^n$ with matrix $A$. The $F[x]$-module $V_T$ is finitely generated (by any basis) and torsion: by Cayley–Hamilton, the characteristic polynomial kills every vector. One can show that $V_T$ has the presentation $F[x]^n/\operatorname{rows}(xI-A^{\mathsf{T}})$ (the relations are $x e_j - \sum_i a_{ij}e_i$, from $Tb_j = \sum_i a_{ij}b_i$), and transposing does not change the minors, so the Smith normal form of the polynomial matrix $xI - A$, computed over the Euclidean domain $F[x]$, gives
$$V_T\cong F[x]/(f_1)\oplus\cdots\oplus F[x]/(f_m),\qquad f_1\mid\cdots\mid f_m,$$
with monic invariant factors $f_i$. Here $f_m$ is the minimal polynomial of $T$, and $f_1\cdots f_m = \det(xI - A)$ is the characteristic polynomial.

A summand $F[x]/(f)$ with $f = x^d + c_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\dots+c_0$ has basis $1, x, \dots, x^{d-1}$, and multiplication by $x$ has the companion matrix of $f$ in that basis. Putting the companion blocks together gives the rational canonical form, valid over every field. Over $\mathbb{C}$, use elementary divisors instead: a summand $\mathbb{C}[x]/((x-\lambda)^e)$ with basis $(x-\lambda)^{e-1},\dots,(x-\lambda),1$ gives a [[jordan|Jordan block]] of size $e$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$. So the Jordan form is the structure theorem over $\mathbb{C}[x]$.

blocks.title: Reading off a Jordan form
blocks.body: Let $A = \begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. Find the invariant factors of $xI - A$ and describe $\mathbb{Q}^3$ as a $\mathbb{Q}[x]$-module.
blocks.solution:
We have $xI - A = \begin{pmatrix}x-2&-1&0\\0&x-2&0\\0&0&x-2\end{pmatrix}$. Use the minors. The entry $-1$ is a unit, so $d_1 = 1$. The $2\times2$ minors include $(x-2)^2$, $-(x-2)$ (rows $1,3$ and columns $2,3$), and $0$; every $2\times2$ minor is divisible by $x-2$, so $d_1d_2 = x-2$. The determinant is $(x-2)^3$, so $d_1d_2d_3 = (x-2)^3$. Hence the Smith form is $\operatorname{diag}\big(1,\ x-2,\ (x-2)^2\big)$ and
$$\mathbb{Q}^3_A\cong\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x-2)\oplus\mathbb{Q}[x]/\big((x-2)^2\big).$$
The minimal polynomial is $(x-2)^2$, the characteristic polynomial $(x-2)^3$, and the Jordan form has blocks of sizes $1$ and $2$ for eigenvalue $2$, which is what $A$ already is. By contrast, $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ gives the single summand $\mathbb{Q}[x]/(x^2+1)$: since $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$, there are no eigenvectors and no smaller invariant subspaces.

blocks.body:
- $\mathbb{Z}/6\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ because $2$ and $3$ are coprime, but $\mathbb{Z}/4\not\cong\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ (the first has an element of order $4$).
- Invariant factors must form a divisibility chain; $\mathbb{Z}/2\oplus\mathbb{Z}/3$ is written as $\mathbb{Z}/6$ in invariant factor form, not as two factors.
- Finite generation matters: $\mathbb{Q}$ is a torsion-free $\mathbb{Z}$-module that is not free (any two rationals are dependent over $\mathbb{Z}$, but $\mathbb{Q}$ is not cyclic). For finitely generated modules over a PID, torsion-free does imply free.
- The PID hypothesis matters: the ideal $(2,x)$ of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$ is a torsion-free $\mathbb{Z}[x]$-module that is not free, since any two elements $f, g$ satisfy the relation $g\cdot f - f\cdot g = 0$ while one element cannot generate it.
- Row operations change the relations but not the module; column operations change the generators. Both are allowed, but only invertible ones over $R$: over $\mathbb{Z}$ you may not divide a row by $2$.

Modules over rings that are not PIDs are studied in [[noetherian-rings]], where finite generation of submodules is built into the definition. The $F[x]$-module viewpoint explains [[jordan|Jordan form]] and the minimal polynomial; modules over a group algebra are [[group-representations]]; and [[tensor-products]] of modules extend the construction for vector spaces. Smith normal form over $\mathbb{Z}$ is the standard algorithm for [[homology]] groups, and the structure theorem for $\mathbb{Z}$-modules describes the finite abelian [[groups]], the [[class-group]] of a number field, and the Mordell–Weil group of an [[elliptic-curves|elliptic curve]].

1. Find the invariant factors of the abelian group with generators $x,y$ and relations $6x+9y = 0$, $12x+6y = 0$.
2. How many abelian groups of order $10^5$ are there up to isomorphism?
3. Show that $\mathbb{Z}/m\oplus\mathbb{Z}/n\cong\mathbb{Z}/\gcd(m,n)\oplus\mathbb{Z}/\operatorname{lcm}(m,n)$.
4. Two $3\times3$ complex matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and the same minimal polynomial. Must they be similar? What about $4\times4$ matrices?
